paragraphs: Training a neural network usually requires derivatives that indicate how its outputs change when its parameters change. Binary and discrete-time spiking networks can have activation functions whose derivatives are unhelpful for this purpose. Surrogate gradient learning substitutes a more usable derivative during training. The paper develops a mathematical framework for understanding why this practical workaround behaves as it does.

The authors build on the neural tangent kernel, a tool for analyzing gradient-based learning. They first examine whether its existing framework can simply accommodate activation functions with jumps. Their analysis shows that ordinary gradient descent remains ill-posed even in the infinite-width limit. They therefore define a surrogate gradient version of the kernel and rigorously extend key supporting theorems.

Numerical experiments illustrate the theory, including a comparison between finite-width networks with sign activations and regression using the new kernel. The reported agreement supports the kernel as a useful characterization of surrogate gradient learning. The contribution is a theoretical foundation tailored to substituted derivatives, backed by numerical evidence connecting it to finite networks.
neurips-2024-a-generalized-neural-tangen.tldr: A generalized neural tangent kernel provides a rigorous framework for analyzing neural networks trained with surrogate derivatives.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms make repeated decisions while receiving feedback about their performance. Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, or FTRL, can adapt to the environment through its regularizer and learning rate. Much of the existing learning-rate work addresses problems whose optimal worst-case regret grows like the square root of the number of rounds. This paper targets a different class, where that growth is proportional to the number of rounds raised to two-thirds.

The proposed learning rate balances three quantities that arise in regret bounds: stability, penalty, and bias. Matching these terms gives a general design principle for adapting FTRL in this harder class of problems. The authors apply it to partial monitoring, graph bandits, and multi-armed bandits in which obtaining observations costs money.

Combined with a Tsallis entropy regularizer, the framework improves existing best-of-both-worlds regret upper bounds. These guarantees address both stochastic and adversarial environments within the same algorithmic approach. The stated benefit is therefore both theoretical and practical in design: improved bounds come from a learning-rate rule that is substantially simpler than earlier rules for this setting.
neurips-2024-a-simple-and-adaptive-learn.tldr: A simple adaptive FTRL learning rate improves best-of-both-worlds regret bounds for several online learning problems with indirect feedback.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning uses an existing dataset to choose how an agent should act. That dataset can create two distinct difficulties: limited observations make the environment hard to estimate, and the environment that produced the data may differ from the one where the agent will operate. The paper develops a single conservative framework for addressing both sources of uncertainty.

The approach uses a distributionally robust Markov decision process. Its central construction is one uncertainty set that accounts for both sparse data and mismatch between the collection and deployment environments. Optimizing the robust policy implements pessimism by accounting for unfavorable possibilities within that set. This ties the treatment of estimation error directly to the treatment of deployment differences.

The authors prove a near-optimal bound on the robust policy's performance gap in the target environment for three uncertainty models: total variation, chi-squared divergence, and KL divergence. Their guarantees match or improve prior results for total variation and KL, and provide the first result for the chi-squared model. The contribution is a unified theoretical treatment across these three ways of describing uncertainty.
neurips-2024-a-unified-principle-of-pess.tldr: A single robust uncertainty set yields near-optimal offline reinforcement learning guarantees that account for both limited data and deployment mismatch.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a language model's size by removing parameters. A central decision is how much to remove from each layer. Assigning every layer the same pruning ratio overlooks differences between layers, while heuristic allocations can produce suboptimal results. AlphaPruning addresses this allocation problem using information contained in the model's weight matrices.

The method draws on Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization theory and examines the shapes of empirical spectral densities of those matrices. The authors' analysis finds substantial variation in how well different layers are trained and, relatedly, how amenable they are to pruning. AlphaPruning uses these shape measurements to assign different sparsity ratios across layers. It can be combined with multiple existing pruning methods.

In the reported experiments, AlphaPruning brings LLaMA-7B to 80% sparsity while retaining what the authors describe as reasonable perplexity. That result supports the value of distributing pruning unevenly according to layer properties. The claim concerns maintaining a useful language-modeling measure at high sparsity; it does not state that removing this many parameters preserves every aspect of model performance.
neurips-2024-alphapruning-using-heavy-ta.tldr: AlphaPruning uses weight-matrix spectral shapes to allocate pruning across layers, reaching 80% sparsity in LLaMA-7B with reasonable perplexity.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making with infinitely many available options whose rewards can deteriorate through use. The setting is rested rotting: an option's mean reward may decrease when selected, but remains unchanged while it is left alone. A learner must therefore judge options using observations that may describe rewards better than those currently available.

The authors consider two ways to constrain deterioration. In the slow-rotting case, the total amount of reward decrease is bounded. In the abrupt-rotting case, the number of deterioration events is bounded. Their algorithm combines an upper-confidence-bound approach with an adaptive sliding window, adjusting which past observations contribute to its estimates.

The window manages a bias–variance trade-off: older observations can become misleading as rewards decline, while relying on fewer observations increases uncertainty. The authors establish tight regret bounds for both rotting scenarios and demonstrate the algorithm numerically. The contribution is one adaptive approach that handles these two different descriptions of reward decay within the stated rested setting.
neurips-2024-an-adaptive-approach-for-in.tldr: An adaptive sliding-window bandit algorithm achieves tight regret bounds when rewards deteriorate through use under either amount-based or event-based constraints.

paragraphs: The paper considers a learner that must collect rewards while satisfying long-term constraints. Its goal is one algorithm with optimal performance whether those constraints arise stochastically or adversarially. Earlier approaches use primal-dual methods and can require demanding assumptions, including Slater's condition and additional knowledge or adaptivity requirements in adversarial settings.

The proposed alternative estimates constraints optimistically, using an approach similar to upper confidence bounds. One component minimizes regret over strategy sets that change over time. Another estimates the feasible set through a weighted empirical average of previous observations. The central design challenge is choosing adaptive weights that satisfy the different requirements of stochastic and adversarial constraints.

The authors show that this approach provides best-of-both-worlds guarantees with logarithmic dependence on the number of constraints, which they identify as a first for this setting. In stochastic environments, it achieves square-root regret up to logarithmic factors without Slater's condition. Together with a simpler algorithm and analysis, these results make optimistic constraint estimation a substantive alternative to the established primal-dual approach.
neurips-2024-beyond-primal-dual-methods-.tldr: Optimistic constraint estimates yield a simpler best-of-both-worlds bandit algorithm with logarithmic dependence on the number of constraints.

paragraphs: Knowing a language model's parameters does not necessarily reveal what proportions of languages, code, or other sources appeared in its training data. This paper studies data mixture inference: estimating those overall proportions instead of identifying individual training examples. Its information source is the byte-pair encoding tokenizer released with a model.

A tokenizer's ordered merge list reflects which byte pairs were frequent as its vocabulary was constructed. Given that list and sample data from categories of interest, the authors formulate a linear program to estimate the categories' relative proportions in the tokenizer's training set. Extending those estimates to model pretraining depends on how representative the tokenizer's data is of the model's data.

Controlled experiments recover known mixtures of natural languages, programming languages, and sources with high precision. Applied to released tokenizers, the method confirms some disclosed information and produces additional inferences about multilingual data, code, and books. Those are indirect corpus estimates subject to the representativeness condition. The work shows that tokenizer construction can expose aggregate information even when the underlying pretraining corpus remains undisclosed.
neurips-2024-data-mixture-inference-atta.tldr: BPE merge lists can reveal tokenizer training mixtures and, when representative, support indirect estimates of a language model's pretraining composition.

paragraphs: Recommenders represent established items using learned patterns of user behavior. Out-of-vocabulary items have only content features, so their representations must be generated from a different source of information. The paper argues that directly mixing these generated representations with established behavioral representations leaves a substantial gap that hurts recommendation quality.

User Sequence IMagination, or USIM, adds a fine-tuning stage that imagines user sequences and uses user behavioral embeddings to refine the generated item embeddings. It formulates this process as reinforcement learning. A recommendation-focused reward assesses how much a user can help recommend an unfamiliar item, while an embedding-driven transition function models how the item representation changes after imagining a user.

Experiments show improvements over traditional generative approaches across both conventional and graph-neural-network-based collaborative filtering models. The authors also report deployment for months on a prominent e-commerce platform serving millions of unfamiliar items and billions of users. The results support refining content-derived embeddings through behavioral information as a useful addition to generating those embeddings in the first place.
neurips-2024-fine-tuning-out-of-vocabula.tldr: USIM uses imagined user sequences to refine content-derived item embeddings and improve recommendations for out-of-vocabulary items.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering can use a graph connecting users and items, with message passing allowing neighboring representations to contribute information. Although this often improves recommendations, the paper questions whether it helps for the same reasons assumed in other graph-learning tasks. The authors investigate the mechanism through theoretical analysis and targeted ablation studies.

They find that the main benefit comes from neighboring representations added during the forward pass, rather than extra gradient updates to neighbors during backpropagation. They also find that message passing usually helps nodes with fewer connections more. These observations motivate TAG-CF, which performs message passing just once at inference time and can augment representations trained with different collaborative-filtering supervision signals.

Across six datasets, TAG-CF improves nongraph collaborative filtering by up to 39.2% for cold users and 31.7% across all users, with little or no extra computational overhead. Against graph-enhanced methods, it achieves comparable or better performance using less than 1% of their total training times. These empirical results support extracting useful graph information at inference without repeatedly incorporating message passing throughout training.
neurips-2024-how-does-message-passing-im.tldr: TAG-CF turns findings about message passing into a single inference-time aggregation step that improves collaborative filtering at low computational cost.

paragraphs: Weight decay regularizes a neural network by applying the same penalty coefficient across its parameters. The paper argues that this uniform treatment may constrain some parameters too strongly and others too weakly. Constrained Parameter Regularization, or CPR, replaces that shared penalty with upper bounds on statistical measures of individual parameter matrices.

For example, CPR can constrain a matrix's L2 norm. Training then becomes a constrained optimization problem, which the authors solve using an adapted augmented Lagrangian method. This changes the role of regularization from applying one constant penalty everywhere to enforcing limits on the chosen matrix statistics. The method introduces only a minor runtime overhead.

CPR requires an upper bound, and the authors propose ways to initialize it that leave either no hyperparameter or one to configure. Experiments in computer vision and language modeling show that CPR can outperform conventional weight decay in both pretraining and fine-tuning. The findings support matrix-level constraints as a practical regularization alternative, with the performance advantage established empirically in the studied tasks.
neurips-2024-improving-deep-learning-opt.tldr: CPR replaces uniform weight decay with matrix-level constraints and can improve pretraining and fine-tuning performance with minor runtime overhead.

paragraphs: Invisible image watermarks embed hidden messages intended to support ownership detection and discourage misuse. This paper examines how robust pixel-level watermarks remain when an image is regenerated. The authors propose a family of attacks that disrupt the hidden signal and then reconstruct the visible image using denoising algorithms or pretrained generative models.

The approach separates watermark destruction from image recovery: random noise damages the watermark, and reconstruction restores image quality. Its flexibility allows different denoising methods and generative models, including diffusion models, to instantiate the same general idea. Formal proofs and empirical evaluations establish vulnerability of pixel-level invisible watermarks to this regeneration approach.

Across four pixel-level watermarking schemes, the method achieves lower detection rates and higher image quality than existing attack techniques in the reported comparisons. The authors identify semantic-preserving watermarks as a possible alternative defense and advocate directing more research toward them. The findings therefore concern a specific weakness of pixel-level invisible signals, while the proposed defensive direction remains an alternative that may resist these attacks.
neurips-2024-invisible-image-watermarks-.tldr: Formal analysis and experiments show that regeneration attacks can remove pixel-level invisible watermarks while retaining high image quality.

paragraphs: A language model can express the same answer in many different ways, so variation in wording is not automatically uncertainty about meaning. This paper focuses on semantic uncertainty, which is relevant when trying to detect factually incorrect responses. It proposes Kernel Language Entropy, or KLE, for models accessed either with or without internal visibility.

KLE represents semantic relationships among outputs using positive semidefinite kernels with unit trace, then measures uncertainty through von Neumann entropy. In practical terms, the representation preserves graded pairwise relationships between answers or groups of answers. This provides finer distinctions than assigning answers to hard semantic clusters and treating those assignments as the whole description of their relationships.

The authors prove that KLE generalizes semantic entropy, the previous state-of-the-art method identified in the abstract. Experiments across multiple generation datasets and model architectures show improved uncertainty quantification. The contribution is a richer mathematical treatment of meaning-level variation, supported by empirical gains in uncertainty estimation. Such estimates are relevant to hallucination detection without making uncertainty itself a guarantee of factual correctness.
neurips-2024-kernel-language-entropy-fin.tldr: Kernel Language Entropy uses graded semantic similarities to improve uncertainty estimates beyond methods based on hard answer clusters.

paragraphs: A vision-language model that answers one question about one image may still struggle in a conversation involving many images and a long history. MMDU evaluates that broader ability, while the accompanying MMDU-45k instruction-tuning dataset aims to improve it. The work moves evaluation beyond short responses and single-choice questions toward extended multimodal dialogue.

The authors cluster related Wikipedia images and descriptions, then construct question-answer pairs through human annotation assisted by GPT-4o. Benchmark examples reach up to 18,000 image-and-text tokens, 20 images, and 27 conversational turns. This scale requires models to follow instructions while retaining relevant information across a substantially longer interaction.

An analysis of 15 representative models finds that open-source systems trail closed-source counterparts, which the authors attribute to limited conversational instruction-tuning data. Fine-tuning on MMDU-45k helps address that gap, producing longer and more accurate conversations. Reported gains also extend to MMStar, MathVista, and ChartQA. The combined benchmark and training resource therefore tests conversational weaknesses and supplies data that empirically helps improve them.
neurips-2024-mmdu-a-multi-turn-multi-ima.tldr: MMDU evaluates extended conversations across multiple images, and MMDU-45k improves open-source vision-language models through instruction tuning.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed data can produce unusually large observations that complicate statistical estimation. Streaming adds memory constraints, making the problem harder than processing a stored batch. This paper formulates high-dimensional streaming estimation as stochastic convex optimization and analyzes Clipped-SGD, which limits the size of gradient updates to control the influence of extreme values.

The authors prove near-optimal sub-Gaussian statistical rates when the stochastic gradient noise has a finite second moment. For smooth, strongly convex objectives, their high-probability bound improves how confidence affects the estimation error. In particular, the confidence-dependent fluctuations are lower order than the main term involving the trace of the clipped-gradient covariance, improving on the previously stated Clipped-SGD rate.

The results also extend to smooth convex and Lipschitz convex objectives. A new iterative refinement technique for martingale concentration supplies the key analytical step. The significance is that a widely used streaming algorithm receives stronger statistical guarantees under a relatively weak moment condition, connecting a practical method for controlling large updates with near-optimal estimation accuracy.
neurips-2024-near-optimal-streaming-heav.tldr: Clipped-SGD achieves near-optimal streaming estimation guarantees for heavy-tailed gradient noise with a finite second moment.

paragraphs: Fourier-based forecasting describes time series through frequency components, but the paper argues that existing methods insufficiently connect those components to their underlying basis functions. The real and imaginary coefficients correspond to cosine and sine functions at different frequencies. Making that relationship explicit matters for interpreting where cycles begin and how representations relate to series length.

The authors introduce Fourier basis mapping, or FBM, which combines time-domain and frequency-domain features through Fourier basis expansion. It incorporates basis functions into the discrete Fourier transform so that explicit frequency information retains temporal characteristics. A mapping network can then learn relationships between timing and frequency instead of treating frequency coefficients without that explicit connection.

FBM is designed as a plug-in for several network families, including linear, multilayer-perceptron, transformer, and Fourier-based models. The authors report state-of-the-art long-term forecasting results on diverse real-world datasets using variants with only one or three fully connected layers. These findings suggest that a more explicit time–frequency representation can deliver strong forecasting performance without requiring a deep mapping network.
neurips-2024-rethinking-fourier-transfor.tldr: Fourier basis mapping explicitly connects frequency coefficients with time, improving long-term forecasting across several neural network families.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning methods can focus on representing the environment, a policy for choosing actions, or a value function describing outcomes. This paper asks whether these targets differ in how difficult they are to represent. That question provides a way to compare major reinforcement learning paradigms through the complexity of what each tries to approximate.

Using time complexity and circuit complexity, the authors identify a potential hierarchy: the environment model is easiest to represent, the optimal policy comes next, and the optimal value function is the most intricate. They also examine the expressive power of multilayer perceptrons and find support for the same ordering, bringing the analysis closer to neural networks used in deep reinforcement learning.

Deep reinforcement learning experiments provide further validation of the theoretical findings. The proposed hierarchy offers a perspective on why different approximation targets can place different demands on a representation. Its scope is representation complexity; the stated findings do not establish that one reinforcement learning paradigm will universally train faster or achieve better decisions in every environment.
neurips-2024-rethinking-model-based-poli.tldr: The paper identifies a potential representation-complexity hierarchy from environment models to optimal policies to optimal value functions.

paragraphs: Observational data can leave several causal graphs indistinguishable, so interventions are needed to resolve their directions. Many causal-discovery policies assume access to unlimited interventional samples. This paper instead considers a Bayesian approach with limited samples, reflecting settings where each intervention produces costly evidence and uncertainty must be tracked explicitly.

The method uses a polynomial-time procedure for uniformly sampling directed acyclic graphs to enumerate possible cut configurations and their interventional distributions for target sets. It tracks posterior probabilities over these possibilities. The algorithm randomly intervenes on target vertex sets that cut every graph edge, then returns a causal graph according to the resulting posteriors.

The authors prove high-probability recovery of the true graph when enough interventional samples are available. Simulated-data comparisons show better structural Hamming distance than the evaluated baselines, indicating closer agreement with the true graph. A separate case study shows how the approach could answer a causal question without recovering the entire graph, including estimating the effect of a variable that cannot itself be intervened on.
neurips-2024-sample-efficient-bayesian-l.tldr: A Bayesian intervention strategy learns causal graphs from limited samples, with high-probability recovery once sufficient evidence is available.

paragraphs: Training large language models across many workers reduces memory pressure, but workers must exchange substantial amounts of weights and gradients. In sharded data parallelism, this communication can limit scalability even though optimizer states are partitioned. SDP4Bit targets that bottleneck by compressing the communicated information while seeking to preserve training quality.

The method reduces communication precision to nearly four bits through two techniques: quantizing weight differences and applying two-level smooth quantization to gradients. It also coordinates the algorithm with runtime optimizations so that compression itself adds less computation. This joint design addresses both the volume of transmitted information and the overhead required to reduce it.

The paper provides convergence guarantees and evaluates GPT pretraining for models with up to 6.7 billion parameters. Those experiments show negligible effects on training loss. Separate speed measurements report up to a 4.08-fold increase in end-to-end throughput on 128 GPUs. These results demonstrate substantial gains in the evaluated configurations while keeping the reported training-loss impact small.
neurips-2024-sdp4bit-toward-4-bit-commun.tldr: SDP4Bit compresses distributed training communication to nearly four bits, with negligible measured training-loss impact and up to 4.08-fold throughput gains.

paragraphs: Many language-model attacks modify ordinary text inputs, an approach that also applies to closed-source systems. This paper examines a different threat enabled by full access to open-source models: modifying the continuous embedding representations associated with input tokens. That access exposes an attack surface that text-only robustness studies do not fully address.

The authors propose embedding-space attacks and find that they bypass alignment and elicit harmful behavior more efficiently than the discrete attacks or model fine-tuning examined in their study. They also show that a model compromised through embeddings can help produce natural-language jailbreaks. This connects a threat involving internal representations with attacks expressed through ordinary text.

The work further tests unlearning, where information is supposed to have been removed from a model. Across multiple datasets and models, embedding attacks extract supposedly deleted information. These findings identify full-model access as an important condition when evaluating safety and unlearning claims: the tested protections can fail when inputs are manipulated in the embedding space rather than only through natural-language prompts.
neurips-2024-soft-prompt-threats-attacki.tldr: Embedding-space attacks expose weaknesses in open-source models' safety alignment and can recover supposedly unlearned information.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, deploying a model can change the data distribution on which its performance is evaluated. This feedback complicates optimization because updates affect both the model and its future data. The paper studies smooth losses that may be nonconvex, extending analysis beyond the strongly convex losses commonly used for greedy deployment with stochastic gradient descent.

The authors introduce stationary performative stable solutions by relaxing the existing performative stability condition. They prove that greedy deployment converges in expectation to a biased version of this target under either of two conditions: Wasserstein-1 sensitivity with loss Lipschitz in the data, or total-variation sensitivity with bounded loss. In both cases, bias scales with gradient variance and distribution-shift sensitivity.

The analysis also covers lazy deployment, where several gradient updates occur between deployments. This scheme converges with reduced bias, showing how deployment frequency can influence stability under model-driven distribution changes. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical results. The guarantees concern these stationary stability targets under the stated conditions, rather than global minimization of a general nonconvex objective.
neurips-2024-stochastic-optimization-sch.tldr: For nonconvex performative prediction, SGD deployment schemes converge toward stationary stability targets, with less frequent deployment reducing bias.

paragraphs: Optical flow estimates motion across video frames. Earlier multi-frame methods often repeat pairwise computations, creating redundant work. StreamFlow introduces a streamlined pipeline that predicts successive one-directional flows together in a single forward pass. The authors report a 44.43% processing-speed increase from this pipeline, reaching efficiency comparable to two-frame networks.

The paper also studies how to use spatial and temporal information within that pipeline. Its Integrative spatiotemporal Coherence method adds parameter-efficient modeling, while a lightweight Global Temporal Regressor incorporates temporal cues. These components improve accuracy, including where parts of a scene are occluded, while adding modest computation to the streamlined processing design.

Relative to the baseline, StreamFlow reports improvements of 15.45% and 11.37% on the Sintel clean and final test sets, with corresponding occluded-region gains of 15.53% and 10.77% and a 1.11% latency increase. It also achieves state-of-the-art cross-dataset results on Sintel and KITTI. Together, the findings support using multi-frame context more efficiently while improving motion estimation and demonstrated cross-domain generalization.
neurips-2024-streamflow-streamlined-mult.tldr: StreamFlow reduces redundant multi-frame processing and adds lightweight temporal modeling to improve optical-flow speed and accuracy.

paragraphs: Vision-language models such as CLIP can recognize objects at the image level across an open vocabulary, but identifying which pixels belong to each object is more difficult. PixelCLIP addresses this gap by adapting CLIP's image encoder for semantic segmentation. Its training uses unlabeled images and region masks rather than semantic labels identifying the contents of those regions.

The masks come from vision foundation models such as SAM and DINO. They provide spatial guidance about where regions are located, but do not supply their semantic identities. To use this information, the authors introduce an online clustering algorithm with learnable class names. The clustering process allows the model to acquire general semantic concepts while receiving guidance about image regions.

The reported results show significant improvements over CLIP and competitive performance against methods trained with captions. The contribution is therefore a way to connect region-level spatial information with open-vocabulary recognition without semantic labels in the adaptation data. It demonstrates that generated masks and learned semantic groupings can help transfer image-level capabilities to pixel-level prediction.
neurips-2024-towards-open-vocabulary-sem.tldr: PixelCLIP combines generated region masks with online clustering to adapt CLIP for open-vocabulary segmentation without semantic labels.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds aim to connect a model's observed performance with its performance beyond training data. Earlier compression-based bounds for language models become uninformative at billion-parameter scale or require compression that yields low-quality text. They also count independent training documents, leaving the much larger number of constituent tokens largely unused in tightening the guarantees.

This paper uses martingale properties to derive bounds that benefit from token counts even though tokens are not independent. That changes the amount of data the analysis can exploit. With many more tokens than documents, the resulting bounds accommodate, and benefit from, less restrictive compression schemes that better preserve useful models.

Using Monarch matrices, Kronecker factorizations, and post-training quantization, the authors obtain non-vacuous bounds for models as large as LLaMA2-70B. They report the first such bounds for models deployed in practice that generate high-quality text. The advance is a theoretical accounting method that makes meaningful guarantees possible at a scale and compression quality where earlier document-based analyses fell short.
neurips-2024-unlocking-tokens-as-data-po.tldr: Martingale-based analysis exploits dependent training tokens to obtain non-vacuous generalization bounds for language models as large as LLaMA2-70B.

paragraphs: Answering a question about an image can depend on noticing a small region within a much larger scene. Multimodal language models can struggle with this localization, especially for high-resolution inputs, and their answers often provide limited interpretability. Visual CoT addresses both issues through a dataset, a processing pipeline, and a benchmark focused on relevant image regions.

The dataset contains 438,000 question-answer pairs with intermediate bounding boxes identifying areas needed to answer the questions. About 98,000 pairs also include detailed reasoning steps. These annotations provide information about both where a model should look and the reasoning associated with answering, going beyond a final answer alone.

The proposed multi-turn pipeline dynamically focuses on visual inputs and produces interpretable reasoning. The benchmark evaluates cases that require identifying particular local regions. Extensive experiments support the framework's effectiveness and inform inference strategies. By pairing localization annotations with reasoning examples, the work offers a concrete resource for studying how models can inspect relevant visual evidence during question answering.
neurips-2024-visual-cot-advancing-multi-.tldr: Visual CoT combines region annotations, reasoning examples, and a multi-turn pipeline to improve interpretable visual question answering.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing changes information held by a model, but evaluating edits becomes more complicated when both images and language are involved. The paper identifies shortcomings in an existing vision-language editing benchmark: unreliable synthesized evaluation images and insufficient assessment of whether edited knowledge is used in related content. VLKEB is designed to improve that evaluation.

The benchmark uses a multimodal knowledge graph to connect images with knowledge entities. These connections allow the authors to extract entity-related information as the basis for editing examples. Alongside the existing reliability, locality, and generality measures, the work extends portability to assess whether an edit carries into relevant content, broadening what successful editing means in the evaluation.

The authors test different editing methods on five large vision-language models and analyze their effects. The results reveal strengths and deficiencies among the evaluated approaches. VLKEB's contribution is a more comprehensive benchmark and a more grounded construction of image-linked editing data, providing a way to study both the immediate edit and its use beyond the directly edited example.
neurips-2024-vlkeb-a-large-vision-langua.tldr: VLKEB links images to knowledge entities and adds portability evaluation to assess knowledge editing across five vision-language models.
